title: Cytokines in Clinical Practice
subject: Medicine
summary: Cytokines are small proteins that mediate inflammation and immune responses. In low‑resource settings they drive sepsis, malaria, TB and HIV complications. Recognising their patterns guides diagnosis, treatment and monitoring.

sections.p: Cytokines are cell‑derived proteins that act locally or systemically to regulate immune and inflammatory responses. Clinically, their effects are inferred from signs of systemic inflammation and laboratory markers such as CRP, pro‑calcitonin and cytokine panels when available.
b: IL‑1, IL‑6, TNF‑α drive fever, capillary leak, and organ dysfunction

t.b: Pro‑calcitonin >0.5 ng/mL supports bacterial sepsis; >2 ng/mL indicates severe sepsis. Useful when cultures are unavailable.
Leukocytosis or neutropenia with left shift suggests bacterial infection; thrombocytopenia may indicate sepsis or malaria.

sections.p: Severity is gauged by organ dysfunction and cytokine‑driven shock. The Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score is practical; a score ≥2 in any organ suggests significant organ injury.

t.b: MAP <65 mmHg despite fluids indicates septic shock; requires vasopressors.
RR >30/min or PaO2/FiO2 <300 indicates acute lung injury.

sections.p: In East Africa, the leading causes of cytokine surge are infections and parasitic diseases. Treat the underlying infection first, then manage the cytokine‑mediated complications.

sections.p: Patients with cytokine storm present with fever, rigors, tachycardia, hypotension, capillary leak, and organ dysfunction. In malaria, jaundice and hemolysis may coexist.

t.b: Sign of capillary leak; assess for third‑spacing.
May indicate hemolysis or hepatic involvement; check bilirubin.

sections.p: Use simple, affordable tests to infer cytokine activity and guide therapy.

Elevated transaminases and bilirubin suggest hepatic involvement or hemolysis.
Creatinine rise indicates acute kidney injury from cytokine‑mediated hypoperfusion.

sections.p: Severe cytokine release can lead to multi‑organ failure, DIC, ARDS, and death if untreated.

t.b: Lactate >2 mmol/L indicates hypoperfusion; >4 mmol/L signals severe shock.
INR >1.5 or DIC panel abnormal suggests consumptive coagulopathy.

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, support organ function, and control the cytokine surge with appropriate drugs and supportive care.

exam: A 28‑year‑old with fever, rigors, and hypotension: what is the first step? — Start broad‑spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour and give crystalloid fluids. A patient with malaria and jaundice: which complication is most likely? — Hemolysis leading to acute kidney injury. Why is pro‑calcitonin useful when cultures are unavailable? — It differentiates bacterial from viral infection and guides antibiotic duration.
